content: Plum pox, also referred to as sharka, is the most destructive viral disease affecting stone fruits within the genus Prunus. This disease is caused by the plum pox virus (PPV), which has multiple strains capable of infecting various stone fruit species, including peaches, apricots, plums, nectarines, almonds, and both sweet and tart cherries. Additionally, wild and ornamental species of Prunus can also be infected by certain strains of the virus. The virus is primarily transmitted by aphids and through the movement of infected plant material to new locations. While plum pox does not pose any health risks to consumers, it significantly impacts the marketability of stone fruits by causing deformities and increased acidity. The only effective method to manage the disease is the destruction of all infected trees, which can result in substantial economic losses. Although a genetically modified plum resistant to the plum pox virus has been developed, it is not yet commercially available. The plum pox virus is a linear, single-stranded RNA virus. There are four recognized strains of the virus: PPV-D, PPV-M, PPV-EA, and PPV-C. Among these, PPV-M is particularly aggressive in peaches, is more efficiently transmitted by aphids, and spreads more rapidly within orchards. PPV-M has also been reported to be seed-transmissible, unlike the other strains. Both PPV-M and PPV-D infect peaches, plums, and apricots, while PPV-C naturally infects sweet and tart cherries and is the only strain known to do so. Experimentally, PPV-C has also infected other Prunus hosts. Several species of aphids can transmit plum pox within orchards and over short distances (200–300 meters) to nearby orchards. Unlike persistent viruses such as barley yellow dwarf virus, PPV is not retained within the aphid but is instead transmitted via the aphid's mouthparts during feeding. Long-distance spread of the virus typically occurs through the movement of infected nursery stock or propagative materials. Once a plant is infected, the virus becomes systemic, residing in the cytoplasm of cells throughout the plant. Infected trees experience a significant reduction in fruit production, and the fruits that are produced are often misshapen and blemished. The presence of plum pox can also exacerbate the effects of other endemic viruses infecting Prunus species, such as prune dwarf virus, Prunus necrotic ringspot virus, and apple chlorotic leaf spot virus, leading to even greater economic losses. In peaches, infected trees may display color-breaking symptoms in blossoms, characterized by darker pink stripes on flower petals, which can aid in early-season surveys. Symptoms may also appear on young leaves in spring or on developing fruit. However, some trees show no visible symptoms on leaves or fruit. Not all infections in Prunus are marked by the characteristic ring symptoms on leaves. Certain cultivars exhibit yellowing line patterns, blotches, or necrotic ring symptoms on expanded leaves, and leaf distortion has also been observed. Infected fruits may develop yellow or brown rings, blotches, or severe deformities, particularly in plums and apricots. The seeds of many infected apricots and some plums may also display ring symptoms. Additionally, many non-Prunus species from at least nine plant families have been artificially infected with one or more strains of the plum pox virus, and some have been found naturally infected in the field. The maintenance of the virus in non-Prunus species complicates disease management efforts. There is no cure or treatment for plum pox once a tree becomes infected. Infected trees must be destroyed to prevent further spread. Once the disease is established, control and prevention measures include field surveys, the use of certified nursery materials, aphid control, and the removal of infected trees from nurseries and orchards. While sources of resistance exist within Prunus, they are uncommon. A team of scientists from the United States and France has genetically engineered a plum variety resistant to plum pox, known as C5. This resistance can be transferred to other plum trees through hybridization. The transgenic plum expresses a plum pox virus coat protein, and the plant produces coat protein mRNA, which is processed by a mechanism called post-transcriptional gene silencing (PTGS). This system functions similarly to the plant's immune system and is mechanistically akin to RNA interference (RNAi). The C5 plum provides a valuable source of germplasm for future breeding programs worldwide. However, similar success has not yet been achieved in genetically modifying other Prunus species, although efforts are ongoing. In the fall of 1999, the PPV-D strain of plum pox was detected in an orchard in Adams County, Pennsylvania, marking the first occurrence of the disease in North America. The infected areas in Pennsylvania were quarantined to prevent the disease's spread, and infected trees were destroyed. Subsequent random surveys in 2000 also detected the virus in Nova Scotia and Southern Ontario, particularly in the Niagara Region. Similar to the United States, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency established quarantine zones in Southern Ontario to prevent the spread of PPV. Despite extensive surveying, the virus has not been found in other areas of Canada with susceptible trees. The Canadian plum pox eradication initiative has involved testing a large number of samples for the virus using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) technology. The University of Guelph's Laboratory Services Division has conducted over 2,000,000 tests in the past five years to support this initiative.
